modules.title: The Hackers-Arise Spine
modules.summary: The attacker curriculum cross-mapped to labs and frameworks: Linux for hackers, TCP/IP for attackers, OSINT tradecraft, password cracking, Wi-Fi hacking, web application exploitation, forensics, SCADA/ICS and satellite — with NICE Framework alignment and safety-critical ethics throughout. Legal targets only.
objectives: Use Linux as an operations platform: bash, text processing at speed.
Map TCP/IP from the attacker's view: recon, scanning, exploitation workflow.
Practice OSINT tradecraft with documentation discipline.
Crack passwords to learn credential hygiene; hack Wi-Fi to learn defense.

notes.title: Linux and networks for hackers
notes.body:
**Linux for hackers**: the hacker-oriented curriculum — bash for operations (loops over targets, parsing output), **text processing at speed** (`grep`/`sed`/`awk`/`cut`/`sort`/`uniq` pipelines on scan output), permissions and SUID (the privesc surface), cron and services (persistence mechanisms — to recognize them).

**Network basics and exploitation**: **TCP/IP for attackers** (what each header field leaks), **reconnaissance** (host discovery, port scanning — connect vs SYN vs UDP), **vulnerability scanning** (service detection, version fingerprinting), the **exploitation workflow** (recon → scan → exploit → post).

- Where labs assume this: if a walkthrough says 'enumerate SMB' and you can't, come back here — the spine fills the gaps
- Scanning discipline: one host deeply before ten hosts shallowly — depth finds the vulnerability
- Document every command — the lab report starts at recon, not at the shell

notes.title: OSINT, passwords, Wi-Fi
notes.body:
**OSINT and reconnaissance**: **passive** (DNS, WHOIS, certificate transparency, breach data, social media) before **active** (anything that touches the target); **tradecraft** (sock puppets, compartmentation); **documentation discipline** (every finding sourced).

**Password cracking**: **hash identification** (hash-identifier thinking), **wordlists and rules** (rockyou + custom rules beat bigger lists), **rig/time estimation** (the math of keyspace ÷ hashrate), **credential hygiene for defenders** (the lesson: length + uniqueness + MFA).

**Wi-Fi hacking**: 802.11 fundamentals, **capture and analysis** (handshakes), WPA handshake attacks (deauth + capture + crack — on YOUR lab network), **defensive countermeasures** (WPA3, PMF, rogue-AP detection).

- Passive before active is ethics AND tradecraft — active recon announces you
- Rule-based cracking: `?d?d?d?d` appends and leetspeak rules multiply a wordlist 100x — attackers think in rules
- Every attack module ends in the defense — that's the spine's contract

notes.title: Web, forensics, OT, NICE
notes.body:
**Web application exploitation**: Burp methodology (proxy → repeater → intruder → decoder), **injection flaws** (SQLi, command injection, XSS — input is the attack surface), **authentication attacks** (brute force, session handling, MFA bypass shapes).

**Forensics for hackers**: disk/memory forensics (what artifacts your attack leaves), **timeline analysis** (super-timelines), **anti-forensics awareness** (know it to detect it).

**SCADA/ICS and satellite**: OT protocols (**Modbus**, DNP3 — unauthenticated by design), ICS attack surface, satellite comms basics — with **safety-critical ethics**: OT attacks can kill. Lab only, air-gapped, never production.

**NICE Framework alignment**: OG (Oversight/Governance), DD (Design/Development), IO (Implementation/Operation), PD (Protection/Defense), IN (Investigation) — map your skills to workforce roles.

cards.back: Passive: no target contact (DNS, OSINT). Active: touches the target (scanning) — announces you, needs authorization.
Rules (append digits, leetspeak) multiply a wordlist ~100x — attackers think in rules, not bigger lists.
Deauth client → capture 4-way handshake → crack offline. Defense: WPA3, PMF.
Proxy (observe) → Repeater (manual) → Intruder (automate) → Decoder. Methodology before automation.
None — unauthenticated by design. OT security is network segmentation + monitoring.
OG Oversight/Governance, DD Design/Development, IO Implementation/Operation, PD Protection/Defense, IN Investigation.

quiz.q: First recon step on a new engagement?
choices: passive: DNS, certs, OSINT — no target contact
quiz.explain: Passive first: it's authorized-safe, silent, and often reveals the attack path.

quiz.q: Hash-identifier says MD5crypt. Best approach?
choices: wordlist + rules (leetspeak, appends) matched to the target's patterns
quiz.explain: Rules multiply the list; target-aware rules (company name, seasons, years) beat raw size.

quiz.q: Deauth attack captured a handshake. Next (legal lab)?
quiz.explain: Offline cracking against your own lab handshake — the authorized workflow.

quiz.q: SQLi found in login form. Professional next step?
choices: document, assess impact minimally, report — stay in scope
quiz.explain: Scope discipline: prove impact minimally, document, report. Scope is the law.

quiz.q: Modbus traffic on an OT network. Defensive priority?
choices: segment the OT network + monitor — protocol can't be secured
quiz.explain: Modbus has no auth — defense is segmentation, allowlisting, and anomaly monitoring.

quiz.q: NICE PD category covers?
choices: Protection and Defense — the blue-team roles
quiz.explain: PD: defend, harden, operate securely — the blue-team workforce roles.

modules.title: Offensive Operations: HTB, THM, OffSec
modules.summary: The penetration-testing track: lab operations methodology (enumeration discipline, privesc patterns, documentation), the PEN-200/OSCP map (methodology, buffer overflows, AD attacks, 24-hour exam logistics), advanced web exploitation (SQLi→RCE, SSRF/cloud metadata, deserialization, race conditions), Active Directory attack chains (Kerberoasting, BloodHound, lateral movement, domain dominance), the T0–T3 CTF architecture, and professional reporting.
objectives: Run the machine methodology: enumerate deeply, exploit methodically, document always.
Execute AD attack chains: Kerberoasting, BloodHound pathfinding, lateral movement.
Chain web vulnerabilities: SQLi→RCE, SSRF→cloud metadata, deserialization.
Write findings that get fixed: severity, evidence, impact, remediation.

notes.title: Lab operations and the OSCP map
notes.body:
**Lab operations**: **machine methodology** (recon → enumerate → exploit → privesc → loot → report), **enumeration discipline** (every port, every service, every version — the vulnerability hides in the boring service), **privesc patterns** (Linux: SUID/cron/writable paths/kernel; Windows: unquoted paths/services/AlwaysInstallElevated/token), **documentation** (screenshots + commands from minute one).

**PEN-200/OSCP map**: the methodology ('try harder' = enumerate more, not guess more), **buffer overflows** (the rite of passage: fuzz → offset → EIP → shellcode → exploit), **AD attacks**, the **24-hour exam** (logistics: sleep strategy, breaks, the report is 48h).

- Enumeration is 70% of the work — the exploit is the receipt, enumeration is the purchase
- Buffer overflows teach the stack: registers, memory layout, DEP/ASLR — the fundamentals disguised as an exploit
- Exam logistics: 24 hours is an ultramarathon — schedule sleep, eat, and start the report early

notes.title: Web chains and AD dominance
notes.body:
**Advanced web**: **SQLi→RCE** (into xp_cmdshell/writing shells), **SSRF** → **cloud metadata** (169.254.169.254 — the keys to the kingdom), **deserialization** (untrusted object graphs = code execution), **race conditions** (TOCTOU — the timing attack).

**AD attack chains**: **Kerberoasting** (request service tickets, crack offline), **AS-REP roasting** (no pre-auth accounts), **BloodHound** methodology (shortest path to Domain Admin — attack the graph, not the host), **lateral movement** (PSExec/WMI/WinRM, pass-the-hash), **domain dominance** (Golden Ticket, DCSync — and the detections each triggers).

- SSRF→metadata is the cloud-native crown jewel — know the IMDSv2 hop-limit defense
- BloodHound: find the path first, exploit second — graph thinking beats host thinking
- Every AD attack has a detection: Kerberoasting → event 4769 anomalies; DCSync → 4662 — red teaches blue

notes.title: CTF architecture and reporting
notes.body:
**T0–T3 challenges**: T0 guided warmups (learn the tool), T1 single-technique (master it), T2 chained scenarios (combine), T3 research-grade (original problems — the frontier).

**Reporting**: finding write-ups (title, severity, CVSS, evidence, business impact, remediation, retest), **risk rating** (likelihood × impact, honestly), **executive summaries** (the page the board reads), **retest verification** (prove the fix).

- A finding without remediation is a complaint — always include the fix
- Risk rating honesty: inflating severity burns credibility; the retest is where trust is earned
- The report is the product — access without a report is a story, not an engagement

cards.back: ~70%. The exploit is the receipt; enumeration is the purchase.
SUID binaries, cron jobs, writable PATH/service files, kernel version, sudo rights.
Request crackable service tickets (RC4) as any user → crack offline → the service account's password.
Attack the graph: shortest path to Domain Admin via misconfigurations, not host-by-host.
169.254.169.254 — instance metadata; IMDSv2 hop limits defend it.
Title, severity/CVSS, evidence, business impact, remediation, retest. Access without a report is a story.

quiz.q: Every port scanned, one obscure UDP service unexamined. Move?
choices: examine the UDP service — vulnerabilities hide in the boring
quiz.explain: Enumeration discipline: the unexamined service is where the vulnerability lives.

quiz.q: AS-REP roasting works against?
quiz.explain: No pre-auth → request the AS-REP directly → crack offline. Harden: enable pre-auth.

quiz.q: Defense against Kerberoasting?
choices: strong (25+ char, random) service passwords + AES; monitor 4769 anomalies
quiz.explain: Crack-resistant service passwords + detection on ticket-request anomalies.

quiz.q: Deserialization of untrusted data gives?
choices: potential code execution — untrusted object graphs
quiz.explain: Gadget chains turn deserialization into RCE — never deserialize untrusted input.

quiz.q: Golden Ticket detection?
choices: anomalous TGT lifetime/encryption + 4769 patterns; monitor DC replication
quiz.explain: Forged tickets betray themselves in ticket metadata and replication events.

quiz.q: Inflating a finding's severity causes?
quiz.explain: Honest risk rating is the currency — the retest is where trust compounds.

modules.title: Defensive Operations: SOC to Incident Response
modules.summary: The blue-team track at SANS depth: SOC operations (L1 triage, L2 investigation/correlation, L3 threat hunting, detection engineering), forensics and incident response (disk/memory/network forensics, the IR lifecycle, chain of custody, timeline analysis), detection engineering (Sigma rules, log sources, tuning), and the Security+ bridge with its readiness gate.
objectives: Triage SOC alerts: L1 speed, L2 depth, L3 hunting.
Run the IR lifecycle: detect → contain → eradicate → recover → lessons-learned.
Write and tune Sigma detections; manage false positives.
Perform timeline analysis with chain-of-custody discipline.

notes.title: SOC operations: the three tiers
notes.body:
**L1 triage**: alert → quick classification (true/false positive, severity) → escalate or close — speed with accuracy. **L2 investigation/correlation**: pull the logs, build the timeline, correlate across sources (EDR + firewall + proxy + identity). **L3 threat hunting**: hypothesis-driven searches ('what would APT-X do here?') — hunts become detections.

**Detection engineering**: hunts that find things become **Sigma rules** (the open detection format); deploy, then **tune** (false positives are the tax — budget for them).

- Triage SLA thinking: time-to-triage is the L1 metric; time-to-contain is the SOC metric
- Correlation > collection: ten log sources mean nothing without joined timelines
- Every hunt documents its hypothesis — failed hunts still teach the environment

notes.title: Forensics and incident response
notes.body:
**Forensics**: disk (file carving, deleted recovery, registry/USN analysis), **memory** (process lists, injected code, network connections — memory is where malware lives), **network** (PCAP timelines, C2 beacons).

**IR lifecycle**: preparation → detection/analysis → **containment** (short-term: isolate; long-term: rebuild) → eradication → recovery → **lessons learned** (the report that prevents recurrence).

**Chain of custody**: hash everything (SHA-256), document every hand — evidence that can't be challenged.

**Timeline analysis**: super-timelines (log2timeline) — the story of the intrusion in one view.

- Contain before eradicating when scope is unknown — the exam and the job agree
- Memory first in live response — it evaporates; disk persists
- Lessons-learned is the deliverable — an IR without it is just firefighting

notes.title: Detection engineering + Security+ bridge
notes.body:
**Sigma rules**: title, logsource, detection (selection + filter + condition), level — write once, convert to Splunk/Elastic/Sentinel. **Log sources and normalization**: know what each source *can't* tell you (the blind spots drive the roadmap). **Tuning**: baseline, threshold, allowlist — false positives tuned, not tolerated.

**Threat-informed defense**: map detections to MITRE ATT&CK — coverage gaps become the hunting backlog.

**Security+ bridge**: SY0-701 defensive vocabulary and the readiness gate — the cert that proves the baseline (full prep in IL-09).

- Sigma: the lingua franca — one rule, many SIEMs
- ATT&CK mapping turns 'we need better detection' into a shopping list
- Tune in production, test in lab — never tune blind

cards.back: L1 triage (speed), L2 investigation/correlation (depth), L3 hunting (hypotheses).
Contain first when scope is unknown — eradication lets attackers re-seed.

cards.front: Live response: memory or disk first?
cards.back: Memory — it evaporates. Disk persists.
Title, logsource, detection (selection/filter/condition), level. One rule, many SIEMs.
Hash (SHA-256) + document every hand — evidence that survives challenge.
Lessons learned — the report that prevents recurrence.

quiz.q: Alert: impossible travel login + new MFA enrollment. L1 action?
choices: escalate to L2 immediately — account takeover pattern
quiz.explain: Impossible travel + MFA change = takeover pattern. Speed matters — escalate.

quiz.q: Ransomware spreading, scope unknown. First?
choices: contain: isolate hosts, kill switch VPN if needed
quiz.explain: Contain the blast radius first — eradication before containment re-seeds.

quiz.q: Sigma rule fires 500x/day, all benign. Move?
choices: tune: baseline, threshold, allowlist — document the change
quiz.explain: Tune, don't tolerate or silently kill — the detection had a reason.

quiz.q: C2 beaconing every 60s in PCAP. Confirm?
choices: regular interval + consistent size + odd JA3 — the beacon pattern
quiz.explain: Beacons: regular intervals, consistent sizes — periodicity analysis confirms.

quiz.q: Detection gap: no logs for cloud control plane. Fix?
choices: enable CloudTrail/org logging — close the blind spot
quiz.explain: You can't detect what you don't log — the blind spot drives the roadmap.

quiz.q: Lessons-learned meeting blames the analyst. Problem?
choices: blameless culture violated — fix the system, not the person
quiz.explain: Blameless postmortems fix systems; blame fixes nothing and hides the next incident.

modules.title: The Forward-Deployed Interface
modules.summary: Security engineering at the customer boundary: the forward-deployed engineer role (embedded with customers, shipping under their constraints), AI-aided security practice (AI in the SOC, AI-assisted threat hunting), professional-certificate preparation, and secure engineering practice — threat modeling, secure defaults, security reviews, shipping safely where the customer watches.
objectives: Operate as a forward-deployed engineer: diagnose, build, and transfer under customer constraints.
Apply AI as a SOC/hunting amplifier — with verification discipline.
Threat-model systems: STRIDE/DREAD as working tools, not compliance theater.
Ship secure defaults and run security reviews that unblock instead of blocking.

notes.title: The FDE role and AI-aided practice
notes.body:
The **forward-deployed engineer** embeds with the customer: their network, their compliance, their timeline. Skills: rapid diagnosis in unfamiliar estates, building to their constraints (air-gapped? regulated?), and **transfer** — the customer must operate it after you leave.

**AI in the SOC**: triage summarization, query generation (KQL from English — then VERIFY), report drafting. **AI-assisted threat hunting**: hypothesis generation from intel, anomaly narration.

- The FDE rule: leave the customer stronger — documentation and handoff are the deliverable
- AI verification discipline: the model drafts, the analyst decides — every AI output gets a human check before action
- Practitioner-led preparation: learn from operators, not lecturers — war stories carry the tacit knowledge

notes.title: Threat modeling as a working tool
notes.body:
**Threat modeling**: enumerate what you're defending, from whom, and where it breaks — **STRIDE** (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, DoS, Elevation) per component; **DREAD** (Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability) for ranking.

- Model early (design phase) — a whiteboard hour saves a sprint of rework
- The output is a mitigations list with owners — a model without mitigations is a diagram
- Revisit on change: new data flow → new model session. Threat models rot like milk, not wine

notes.title: Secure defaults and shipping safely
notes.body:
**Secure defaults**: deny-by-default, least privilege out of the box, safe APIs that are hard to misuse. **Security review**: the review that unblocks — findings with fixes, SLAs by severity, security as a service to engineering.

**Shipping safely at the boundary**: the customer's auditors, their change windows, their rollback needs — security that ships is better than perfect security that doesn't.

- Defaults decide outcomes: most breaches exploit the default, not the exotic
- Review SLA: critical findings in hours, highs in days — predictability builds trust
- At the boundary, your security must survive their procurement — document like an auditor reads it

cards.back: Transfer — the customer operates it after you leave. Docs + handoff.
Model drafts, analyst decides — verify every AI output before action.
Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, DoS, Elevation — per component.
Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability — ranking.
Mitigations with owners — a model without mitigations is a diagram.
Deny-by-default, least privilege OOTB, safe APIs hard to misuse.

quiz.q: Customer is air-gapped and regulated. FDE approach?
choices: build to their constraints: offline, auditable, transferable
quiz.explain: Forward-deployed means their constraints rule — air-gapped, auditable, handoff-ready.

quiz.q: AI drafts an incident summary with a wrong timestamp. Lesson?
choices: verify before action — the analyst decides
quiz.explain: Verification discipline: AI accelerates, humans authorize.

quiz.q: New payment flow added. Threat model?
choices: new data flow → new model session
quiz.explain: Models rot on change — new flows get new sessions.

quiz.q: STRIDE 'R' example?
choices: attacker denies sending the transaction — need non-repudiation (signatures, logs)
quiz.explain: Repudiation: dispute of actions — counter with signed logs and audit trails.

quiz.q: Security review blocks releases for weeks. Fix?
choices: findings with fixes + SLAs by severity — unblock, don't just block
quiz.explain: Reviews as a service: predictable SLAs turn security from gate to partner.

modules.title: Security Operations on Microsoft Sentinel: SC-200
modules.summary: Hunt in KQL, respond in minutes: managing the security operations environment (Defender XDR unified portal, Sentinel workspaces/data connectors/ingestion, analytics rules and automation playbooks, MITRE ATT&CK mapping), incident response across Defender/M365/Purview with Graph enrichment, threat hunting in KQL and notebooks — capped by a live-hunt capstone and SC-200 exam prep.
objectives: Manage the SecOps environment: Sentinel workspaces, connectors, analytics rules, playbooks.
Respond to incidents across Defender XDR, Endpoint, M365, Purview.
Hunt in KQL: hypotheses first, queries second, notebooks for repeatability.
Execute the live-hunt capstone: detect → investigate → contain → report.

notes.title: The security operations environment
notes.body:
**Defender XDR**: the unified portal (incidents queue, advanced hunting). **Sentinel**: **workspaces** (the data boundary), **data connectors** (Defender, Entra, firewalls, CEF/Syslog), ingestion planning (cost follows volume — filter at the source).

**Analytics rules**: scheduled KQL (the detection), NRT (near-real-time for the urgent), **automation playbooks** (Logic Apps: enrich → notify → contain).

**MITRE ATT&CK mapping** — exam weight 40–45%: map every rule to technique; coverage gaps are the roadmap.

- Connector first, rule second — detections need data
- Playbooks: SOAR without the buzzword — enrich the incident, then act (isolate device, revoke session)
- Cost discipline: ingestion is metered — high-volume noise gets filtered or sampled, never blindly ingested

notes.title: Incident response across the stack
notes.body:
**Defender XDR + Endpoint**: incidents (correlated alerts), device timelines, live response. **M365/Purview**: email (phishing), Teams/SharePoint, DLP and insider risk.

**Microsoft Graph for enrichment**: query identity, device, risk state programmatically — the API behind the portal.

**Security Copilot as an assistant** — drafts summaries and queries; the analyst verifies (the AI discipline, again).

- Incident queue triage: true positive? severity? blast radius? — the L1/L2 motion in Sentinel
- Live Response: run commands on the endpoint from the portal — contain without touching the desk
- Exam weight 35–40%: the response workflow is the exam's heart — know the portal cold

notes.title: Threat hunting, capstone, exam prep
notes.body:
**KQL deeply**: `SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4688 | summarize count() by Process` — then joins (`join kind=inner`), time charts (`summarize by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)`), anomaly patterns.

**Hypotheses first**: 'if the attacker used X, we'd see Y in table Z' — then the query. **Notebooks** (Jupyter in Sentinel): repeatable hunts, shared tradecraft.

**Live-hunt capstone**: a multi-stage attack scenario — detect, investigate, contain, report. No new tools: synthesis only. The incident report is the deliverable.

**SC-200 prep**: read the KQL before the answers (the exam tests query comprehension); portal-navigation familiarity; triage prioritization; logistics.

cards.back: The data boundary — connectors ingest, rules query, costs accrue here.
Scheduled (KQL batch), NRT (near-real-time), plus playbook automation.
Environment + ATT&CK mapping, 40–45% — connectors, rules, playbooks.
Hypothesis first: 'if X, we'd see Y in Z' — then the query, then the notebook.
Run commands on endpoints from the Defender portal — contain remotely.
Filter at the source — metered ingestion punishes noise.

quiz.q: Phishing wave hits M365. Sentinel workflow?
choices: connector (M365) → analytics rule → playbook (enrich, isolate, notify)
quiz.explain: Data → detection → automation: the Sentinel incident pipeline.

quiz.q: KQL: top processes spawning cmd.exe?
choices: SecurityEvent | where Process has 'cmd.exe' | summarize count() by ParentProcessName | top 10 by count_
quiz.explain: Filter, aggregate by parent, rank — the hunting query shape.

quiz.q: Incident severity: ransomware on 3 hosts vs phishing click, no payload?
choices: ransomware critical (blast radius); phishing low (verify, monitor)
quiz.explain: Triage by blast radius and stage — prioritize the active intrusion.

quiz.q: Copilot suggests isolating the DC. Move?
choices: verify the hypothesis first — DC isolation is blast-radius-critical
quiz.explain: AI assists, analyst authorizes — especially for infrastructure-critical actions.

quiz.q: ATT&CK-mapped rule coverage shows gaps in Defense Evasion. Next?
choices: hunt + write detections for the gap techniques
quiz.explain: Gaps become the hunting/detection backlog — threat-informed defense.

quiz.q: Playbook triggers on every benign admin logon. Fix?
choices: tune the analytics rule: allowlist admin patterns, tighten KQL
quiz.explain: Tune the detection — automation amplifies both signal and noise.

scriptLabs.title: Recon Pipeline: Passive-First Scripting
scriptLabs.brief: Build a passive recon script: given a domain, pull certificate transparency (crt.sh), DNS records, and WHOIS — no packets to the target. Required fragments enforce the passive discipline.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Passive recon: crt.sh + DNS + WHOIS. No active scanning."""
import json, subprocess, sys, urllib.request

domain = sys.argv[1]
# TODO 1: crt.sh JSON for subdomains
# TODO 2: DNS records via dig (A, MX, TXT)
# TODO 3: WHOIS registrar + dates
# print a findings report
scriptLabs.hint: crt.sh: https://crt.sh/?q=%.domain&output=json. dig +short. whois | grep -i registrar. All passive — nothing touches the target's ports.
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Passive recon: crt.sh + DNS + WHOIS. No active scanning."""
import json, subprocess, sys, urllib.request

domain = sys.argv[1]
print(f'=== passive recon: {domain} ===')

# 1. Certificate transparency: subdomains from public logs (fully passive)
url = f'https://crt.sh/?q=%.{domain}&output=json'
try:
    data = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30))
    subs = sorted({e['name_value'] for e in data})
    print(f'--- crt.sh: {len(subs)} names ---')
    print('\n'.join(subs[:50]))
except Exception as ex:
    print('crt.sh failed:', ex)

# 2. DNS via the resolver (not the target)
for rtype in ('A', 'MX', 'TXT', 'NS'):
    out = subprocess.run(['dig', '+short', domain, rtype], capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(f'--- DNS {rtype} ---\n{out.stdout.strip() or "(none)"}')

# 3. WHOIS: registrar and dates
out = subprocess.run(['whois', domain], capture_output=True, text=True)
for line in out.stdout.splitlines():
    if any(k in line.lower() for k in ('registrar:', 'creation date', 'expiry')):
        print('WHOIS:', line.strip())
print('=== done: zero packets to target ports ===')

scriptLabs.title: Sigma: Hunt Becomes Detection
scriptLabs.brief: Write a Sigma rule detecting suspicious PowerShell (encoded commands / download cradles), with logsource, detection logic, and level. Then write the tuning note: what would false-positive and how you'd filter it.
scriptLabs.starter:
title: Suspicious PowerShell Encoded Command
# TODO: id, status, description, logsource (windows, sysmon), detection (selection + filter + condition), level
# TODO: falsepositives + a tuning filter
scriptLabs.hint: selection: EventID 1 (Sysmon) or 4688; CommandLine contains '-EncodedCommand' or 'IEX' or 'DownloadString'. filter: known admin tools. condition: selection and not filter.
scriptLabs.solution:
title: Suspicious PowerShell Encoded Command
id: 11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555
status: test
description: Detects PowerShell with -EncodedCommand or download cradles (IEX/DownloadString) - common attacker tradecraft.
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-EncodedCommand'
      - '-enc '
      - 'IEX'
      - 'DownloadString'
      - 'Invoke-Mimikatz'
  filter_admin:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'SCCM_EncodedDeploy'   # known admin tooling marker
  condition: selection and not filter_admin
falsepositives:
  - Admin automation using encoded commands
  - Software deployment tools
level: high
# TUNING NOTE: baseline for 2 weeks; allowlist the deployment tool's exact
# command-line marker; escalate level to critical if paired with
# network connection to rare external IP (correlation rule).

scriptLabs.title: KQL Hunt: Impossible Travel
scriptLabs.brief: Write a KQL query finding impossible-travel logons: same user, two distant locations, within 60 minutes. Required fragments force the self-join pattern.
scriptLabs.starter:
// TODO: SigninLogs, two logons same user, different cities, < 60 min apart
// HINT: join the table to itself on UserPrincipalName, filter time delta and location difference
scriptLabs.hint: A=SigninLogs | where ResultType==0; B=A; A | join kind=inner (UserPrincipalName) B | where A.TimeGenerated < B.TimeGenerated and datetime_diff('minute', A.TimeGenerated, B.TimeGenerated) between (1..60) and A.LocationDetails.city != B.LocationDetails.city
scriptLabs.solution:
let window = 60; // minutes
SigninLogs
| where ResultType == 0  // successful logons only
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, City = LocationDetails.city, IPAddress
| join kind=inner (
    SigninLogs
    | where ResultType == 0
    | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, City = LocationDetails.city, IPAddress
  ) on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated < TimeGenerated1
| where datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, TimeGenerated1) between (1 .. window)
| where City != City1
| project UserPrincipalName, FirstCity=City, FirstTime=TimeGenerated, SecondCity=City1, SecondTime=TimeGenerated1,
    MinutesApart=datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, TimeGenerated1)
| order by MinutesApart asc
// Tune: allowlist VPN egress cities; alert on <30 min intercontinental pairs first.

scenarios.title: The Phishing Wave
scenarios.context: Monday 8 AM: 40 users report a credential-harvesting email. Three clicked.

options.text: Pull the email, extract URLs/attachments, hunt who clicked, force password resets + revoke sessions for clickers
options.why: Contain the credential compromise first: identify clickers, kill their sessions, reset — before the attacker uses them.
Communication matters but containment is first — the attacker is inside the 15-minute window.
One domain blocked; the campaign rotates in minutes. Hunt the clicks, not just the sender.

options.text: Search mail logs for all recipients, pull the payload, check for payload execution (EDR), hunt lateral movement
options.why: Scope the incident: everyone who got it, anyone who ran it, any movement. Then lessons-learned.
Containment isn't resolution — scope, eradicate, recover, learn.

scenarios.title: BloodHound Finds a Path
scenarios.context: BloodHound shows: helpdesk tier → local admin on workstation → DA in 3 hops via unconstrained delegation.

options.text: Follow the shortest path: compromise the chain step by step, documenting each hop
options.why: Graph thinking: exploit the path, document each hop for the report — that's the finding.
Ignoring the path wastes the intel — the path IS the vulnerability.

steps.prompt: As the defender reading this report, you fix?

options.text: Remove unconstrained delegation, tier the admin model, monitor the path — fix the graph, not the host
options.why: The vulnerability is architectural — delegation + tiering flaws. Host fixes don't close graph paths.
Reimaging one node leaves the delegation path intact for the next workstation.

blocks.body: Passive → active recon → enumerate deeply (70%) → exploit → privesc (SUID/cron/paths) → loot → document from minute one
Kerberoasting (4769) · AS-REP roast (no pre-auth) · BloodHound shortest path · lateral (PSExec/WMI) · Golden Ticket/DCSync = domain dominance
Burp: proxy→repeater→intruder · SQLi→RCE · SSRF→169.254.169.254 (IMDSv2 defends) · deserialization = RCE · race = TOCTOU
Legal targets only · documented authorization · stay in scope · report with remediation · responsible disclosure
L1 triage (speed) → L2 correlate (depth) → L3 hunt (hypotheses) · contain before eradicate · memory before disk
Sigma: title/logsource/detection/level · hunts become rules · tune FPs, don't tolerate · ATT&CK maps the gaps
Prepare → detect → contain → eradicate → recover → lessons-learned · chain of custody: hash + document · blameless postmortems
Hypothesis first · join for impossible travel · connectors before rules · playbooks: enrich→act · filter ingestion at source

answerBank.q: How do I start in cybersecurity with no background?
answerBank.a: The spine: Linux + networking + the Security+ bridge (Module 1 + Module 3's gate), then pick red or blue. Labs on legal targets from day one — reading without doing doesn't transfer in security.

As a methodology credential, yes — it's the most respected hands-on cert in pentesting. Budget 3-6 months of lab time. This module maps PEN-200's methodology; the exam itself is OffSec's 24-hour practical.
Learn both basics, then follow the work you can't stop doing: hunters love the chase (blue), breakers love the puzzle (red). The market needs both; the module trains both so you choose informed.

answerBank.q: Is AI going to replace SOC analysts?
answerBank.a: No — it amplifies them. AI drafts summaries and queries; analysts verify, decide, and handle the novel. The module's AI discipline (verify before action) is the skill that keeps you employed.
Possible but painful — get AZ-900-level Azure familiarity first, then the module's KQL depth. The exam is 40%+ environment/ATT&CK mapping; portal fluency matters as much as query skill.

answerBank.q: What's the single highest-value defensive skill?
answerBank.a: Detection engineering: turning hunts into Sigma rules tuned to your environment. It's the bridge between red knowledge and blue operations — and it's chronically understaffed.
